lesson_title: Balloons and Tug-of-War: Molecular Shapes and Polarity
hook_text: Tie four balloons together and they form the exact shape of methane. Molecules obey balloon rules.
clip_script: Tie four balloons together at their necks and let go. They don't sit flat — they spring into a three-legged stool with one balloon pointing up. A tetrahedron. Now here's the wild part: that is EXACTLY the shape of methane, and for the same reason. Electron pairs around an atom all carry negative charge, so they shove each other as far apart as they can get — balloons in miniature. Two pairs? A straight line, like carbon dioxide. Four pairs? The stool, 109,5 degrees. But some balloons are invisible: lone pairs shove like everyone else, yet no atom sits at their corner. Ammonia hides one balloon and looks like a pyramid. Water hides two and looks bent — just three atoms at an angle. And that bend changes the world. Every bond is a tug-of-war for electrons: oxygen out-pulls hydrogen, so each of water's bonds has a negative end and a positive end. In straight carbon dioxide, the two pulls cancel perfectly. In BENT water, they can't — the whole molecule ends up with a charged side. That bend is why water dissolves salt, sticks to glass, and boils hot enough for tea. Geometry, running chemistry.
visual_style: Real balloons snapping into a tetrahedron, morphing into glowing electron clouds around atoms; lone pairs rendered as ghost balloons fading from view; tug-of-war ropes over bonds with a final bent water molecule glowing charged blue and red.
mood: Hands-on and surprising — party balloons quietly explaining the universe.
pacing: Playful physical open, clean shape-by-shape middle, resonant landing on the bent molecule that runs the world.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never draw a wrong molecular shape again.
